_about: Hand-written key points for pyt-pathology.html (27 Nov 2026, lead). Samples: FMGE recalls, no images.
subject: Pathology
intro: Pathology in FMGE is mostly recognition: the classic cell, body or stain, the gene behind a cancer, and the blood picture of each anaemia. These are the topics that keep coming back, most-asked first, with the one thing to remember about each.

path.cell.rev.note: Reversible injury: cell swelling (the earliest change), fatty change, blebs. Irreversible: mitochondrial damage, membrane rupture, nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis). Adaptations: hypertrophy (bigger cells), hyperplasia (more cells), atrophy, metaplasia (one adult cell type replaced by another).
path.cell.rev.why: An increase in cell size is hypertrophy; an increase in cell number is hyperplasia.

path.cell.nec.note: Coagulative: most infarcts (heart, kidney); outlines kept. Liquefactive: brain infarcts and abscesses. Caseous: TB. Fat necrosis: pancreatitis and breast (chalky deposits). Fibrinoid: vasculitis and malignant hypertension. Gangrene: wet (infected) or dry.
path.cell.nec.why: Preserved cell outlines with fading nuclei in an infarct are coagulative necrosis.

path.cell.apo.note: Programmed cell death without inflammation: shrinkage, condensed chromatin, apoptotic bodies. Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway: cytochrome c release, BCL-2 family control it; extrinsic: Fas and TNF receptors. Caspases carry it out. Councilman bodies in hepatitis are apoptotic cells.
path.cell.apo.why: Cytochrome c release from mitochondria activates the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis.

path.infl.acute.note: Histamine (from mast cells) causes the first vasodilation and leakiness. Neutrophils arrive first (6-24 hours), then macrophages. Steps: margination, rolling (selectins), adhesion (integrins), transmigration (PECAM-1), chemotaxis (C5a, IL-8, LTB4). Fever: IL-1, IL-6, TNF. Albumin falls (negative acute phase protein); CRP and ferritin rise.
path.infl.acute.why: Histamine is the main early mediator of vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

path.infl.chronic.note: Granuloma: a collection of epithelioid macrophages, often with giant cells (Langhans in TB, foreign body type). Formed by type IV (T-cell) hypersensitivity with IFN-γ. Caseating: TB; non-caseating: sarcoidosis, Crohn disease.
path.infl.chronic.why: TB granulomas are a type IV, T-cell mediated reaction.

path.infl.heal.note: Order: inflammation, then proliferation (granulation tissue, angiogenesis by VEGF), then remodelling. Type III collagen first, replaced by type I. Scar strength reaches about 70-80% of normal at 3 months. Vitamin C and zinc are needed; keloids extend beyond the wound edge.
path.infl.heal.why: Healing goes inflammation, then proliferation, then remodelling.

path.haem.anem.note: Haemolysis: low haptoglobin, high LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, reticulocytosis. Sickle cell: HbS (valine for glutamic acid at position 6), crises with bone pain. Hereditary spherocytosis: osmotic fragility, high MCHC, cured by splenectomy. G6PD: Heinz bodies, bite cells after oxidant drugs. Thalassaemia: target cells, HbA2 raised in trait.
path.haem.anem.why: Recurrent bone pain crises with anaemia and jaundice in a child point to sickle cell anaemia.

path.haem.leuk.note: AML: Auer rods, MPO positive; M3 (APML) t(15;17), DIC, ATRA. ALL: TdT positive, PAS positive; children. CML: t(9;22) Philadelphia, low LAP score. CLL: smudge cells, CD5 positive B cells. Hairy cell: TRAP positive, CD11c, CD25, CD103, dry tap, big spleen.
path.haem.leuk.why: CD11c, CD25 and CD103 together mark hairy cell leukaemia.

path.haem.lym.note: Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15, CD30); nodular sclerosis is the commonest type, lymphocyte-rich has the best outlook. Non-Hodgkin: Burkitt t(8;14) c-MYC, starry sky; follicular t(14;18) BCL-2; mantle cell t(11;14) cyclin D1. An excision biopsy of the whole node is the diagnostic test.
path.haem.lym.why: Lymphoma needs a whole-node biopsy to see the architecture; FNAC is not enough.

path.haem.pc.note: Multiple myeloma: CRAB (high Calcium, Renal failure, Anaemia, Bone lytic lesions), M spike, Bence Jones protein, rouleaux, punched-out skull lesions, plasma cells over 10% in marrow. Waldenström: IgM, hyperviscosity.
path.haem.pc.why: Hypercalcaemia is the C in the CRAB criteria for myeloma.

path.haem.mpn.note: Polycythaemia vera: JAK2 V617F, high red cell mass, low erythropoietin, itching after a bath. Essential thrombocythaemia: platelets over 450,000. Primary myelofibrosis: teardrop cells, leucoerythroblastic picture, dry tap, huge spleen. CML: BCR-ABL.
path.haem.mpn.why: Teardrop cells, nucleated red cells and marrow fibrosis make up primary myelofibrosis.

path.neo.onc.note: Oncogenes need one hit (gain of function): RAS (commonest), MYC, HER2/neu, BCR-ABL, RET, KIT. Tumour suppressors need two hits (loss of function). Point mutation (RAS), amplification (MYC, HER2) and translocation (BCR-ABL) switch oncogenes on.
path.neo.onc.why: A growth signal that stays on without its ligand comes from an activated oncogene.

path.neo.tsg.note: p53 (guardian of the genome): stops the cell cycle at G1/S to allow repair, or triggers apoptosis; the commonest mutated gene in cancer; Li-Fraumeni. RB: retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma (two-hit hypothesis). APC: familial polyposis. BRCA1/2: breast and ovary. NF1, WT1, VHL.
path.neo.tsg.why: p53 halts the cell cycle after DNA damage so it can be repaired (or the cell dies).

path.neo.mol.note: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2), microsatellite instability, right-sided colon cancers, endometrial cancer. Familial polyposis: APC, hundreds of polyps. BRCA defects: homologous recombination repair.
path.neo.mol.why: Lynch syndrome comes from defective DNA mismatch repair, which shows as microsatellite instability.

path.neo.met.note: Carcinomas spread by lymph; sarcomas by blood (exceptions: renal cell, liver and follicular thyroid cancers spread by blood). Bone metastases: breast, prostate (osteoblastic), lung, kidney, thyroid. The commonest malignant liver tumour is a metastasis.

path.imm.hs.note: Type I: IgE and mast cells (anaphylaxis, asthma, hay fever). Type II: antibodies against cells (transfusion reactions, Goodpasture, myasthenia, Graves). Type III: immune complexes (SLE, serum sickness, post-strep GN, Arthus). Type IV: T cells (TB granuloma, Mantoux, contact dermatitis, graft rejection).

path.imm.auto.note: Goodpasture: anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen, lung bleeding and nephritis (linear IgG on immunofluorescence). SLE: anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith. Sjögren: anti-Ro and anti-La. Most autoimmune diseases are commoner in women.
path.imm.auto.why: Haemoptysis with haematuria and anti-GBM antibodies is Goodpasture syndrome.

path.imm.tx.note: Hyperacute rejection (minutes): pre-formed antibodies, type II. Acute (weeks to months): T cells and antibodies; treatable. Chronic (months to years): vascular narrowing and fibrosis. Graft-versus-host disease: donor T cells attack skin, gut and liver, after bone marrow transplants.

path.hemo.coag.note: PT tests the extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and warfarin; aPTT tests the intrinsic pathway (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and heparin. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT first (factor VII has the shortest half-life); haemophilia prolongs only aPTT. Bleeding time tests platelets.
path.hemo.coag.why: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs PT; haemophilia A leaves PT normal.

path.hemo.dis.note: von Willebrand disease: the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, long bleeding time with long aPTT. DIC: low platelets and fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes. TTP: ADAMTS13 deficiency (pentad: fever, low platelets, haemolysis, kidney, brain). ITP is the commonest reason for elective splenectomy.
path.hemo.dis.why: Chronic ITP that fails medical treatment is the commonest indication for an elective splenectomy.

path.hemo.thr.note: Virchow triad: endothelial injury, stasis, hypercoagulability. Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited cause of a clotting tendency. Lines of Zahn show a clot formed in flowing blood (before death). Leg vein clots travel to the pulmonary arteries.
path.hemo.thr.why: A clot from the leg veins travels through the right heart and lodges in the pulmonary artery.

path.gen.chr.note: Trisomy 21 Down; trisomy 18 Edwards (rocker-bottom feet, clenched hands); trisomy 13 Patau (cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly). 45,XO Turner; 47,XXY Klinefelter. Prader-Willi (paternal deletion) and Angelman (maternal deletion) of 15q are imprinting disorders.
path.gen.chr.why: Cleft lip and palate with intellectual disability points to Patau syndrome (trisomy 13).

path.gen.tech.note: FISH: finds specific deletions and translocations. Karyotyping: whole-chromosome changes. PCR amplifies DNA; RT-PCR, RNA. Southern blot: DNA; Northern: RNA; Western: protein. Microarrays find small copy-number changes.

path.cvs.mi.note: Changes over time: coagulative necrosis by 4-12 hours, neutrophils 1-3 days, macrophages 3-7 days (rupture risk highest at 3-7 days), granulation tissue 1-2 weeks, scar by 2 months. TTC stain shows the infarct pale against red healthy muscle in the first hours.
path.cvs.mi.why: Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stains living muscle red and leaves the infarct pale.

path.cvs.ie.note: Acute: Staph aureus on normal valves (IV drug users: tricuspid). Subacute: viridans strep on damaged valves. Signs: Osler nodes (painful), Janeway lesions (painless), Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages. Diagnosis: Duke criteria, blood cultures and echo.

path.cvs.rf.note: Follows group A strep throat infection by 2-3 weeks (molecular mimicry). Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells. Jones criteria: carditis, arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules. Mitral valve is most affected.
path.cvs.rf.why: Aschoff bodies contain Anitschkow cells with caterpillar-shaped nuclei; they are the mark of rheumatic carditis.

path.ren.nephrotic.note: Minimal change: children, podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, steroid-responsive. FSGS: commonest in adults in many places, HIV and heroin. Membranous: adults, spike and dome on silver stain, PLA2R antibodies. Diabetic: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.
path.ren.nephrotic.why: Spike-and-dome capillary walls on silver stain are membranous nephropathy.

path.ren.nephritic.note: Haematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, oedema. Post-strep: subepithelial humps, low C3. IgA nephropathy: haematuria 1-2 days after a sore throat, the commonest GN worldwide. Rapidly progressive (crescents): Goodpasture, ANCA vasculitis, immune complex. Alport: collagen IV, deafness, eye changes.

path.ren.dn.note: The earliest change is thickening of the glomerular basement membrane; then mesangial expansion and Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis). Microalbuminuria is the first clinical sign. Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of both arterioles.

path.liv.hep.note: Viral hepatitis: ballooning degeneration, Councilman (acidophil) bodies, ground-glass cells in hepatitis B. Alcoholic hepatitis: Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophils, AST:ALT over 2. Autoimmune hepatitis: plasma cells, interface hepatitis.

path.liv.cirr.note: Diffuse fibrosis with regenerating nodules. Causes in India: alcohol, hepatitis B and C, fatty liver. Leads to portal hypertension, liver failure and hepatocellular cancer. Wilson (copper) and haemochromatosis (iron, Prussian blue) are inherited causes.

path.liv.hcc.note: Risk: hepatitis B and C, cirrhosis, aflatoxin (p53 mutation). AFP rises and is used to monitor treatment. Spreads through the blood (portal vein invasion). Fibrolamellar variant: young adults, normal AFP, better outlook.
path.liv.hcc.why: AFP is the tumour marker for hepatocellular carcinoma and is used to follow treatment.

path.lung.copd.note: Emphysema: centriacinar in smokers (upper lobes), panacinar in α1-antitrypsin deficiency (lower lobes). Neutrophil elastase and MMP-12 destroy elastin. Chronic bronchitis: Reid index over 0.4 (mucous gland hyperplasia).
path.lung.copd.why: Neutrophil elastase and macrophage MMP-12 break down alveolar elastin in COPD.

path.lung.ild.note: Usual interstitial pneumonia (IPF): patchy fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, honeycombing at the bases. Sarcoid: non-caseating granulomas, asteroid and Schaumann bodies. Asbestosis: ferruginous bodies. Silicosis: nodules in the upper lobes.

path.lung.ca.note: Adenocarcinoma: the commonest type overall and in non-smokers, peripheral, glands and mucin (EGFR, ALK). Squamous: central, smokers, keratin pearls, PTHrP (high calcium). Small cell: central, neuroendocrine, ADH (low sodium) and ACTH, Lambert-Eaton.
path.lung.ca.why: High calcium in a smoker with a lung mass points to squamous cell carcinoma making PTHrP.

path.gi.barrett.note: Intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus (goblet cells replacing squamous lining) from long-standing reflux. Raises the risk of adenocarcinoma; followed with endoscopy and biopsy.

path.gi.gastric.note: Intestinal type: H. pylori, glands, older men. Diffuse type: signet ring cells, linitis plastica (leather bottle stomach), E-cadherin loss. Spread: Virchow node, Krukenberg tumour (ovaries), Sister Mary Joseph nodule.

path.gi.ibd.note: Crohn: transmural, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, fistulas, creeping fat. Ulcerative colitis: mucosal, continuous from the rectum, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps. Faecal calprotectin and lactoferrin show bowel inflammation.
path.gi.ibd.why: Faecal lactoferrin comes from neutrophils in the bowel and marks intestinal inflammation.

path.gi.crc.note: Adenoma-carcinoma sequence: APC loss first, then KRAS, then p53. Villous adenomas carry the highest cancer risk. Right-sided cancers bleed (anaemia); left-sided ones obstruct. CEA for follow-up.
path.gi.crc.why: Loss of APC is the first step in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

path.endo.thy.note: Papillary: commonest, Orphan Annie nuclei, nuclear grooves, psammoma bodies, lymph node spread, radiation link. Follicular: capsule and vessel invasion, spreads by blood. Medullary: C cells, calcitonin, amyloid, MEN2 (RET). Anaplastic: elderly, fatal. Hashimoto: Hürthle cells, lymphocytes, risk of lymphoma.
path.endo.thy.why: Medullary thyroid cancer with phaeochromocytoma and mucosal neuromas is MEN2B, from RET mutations.

path.tl.title: Must-memorise translocations
path.tl.note: t(9;22) CML (BCR-ABL); t(15;17) acute promyelocytic leukaemia (PML-RARA); t(8;14) Burkitt (c-MYC); t(14;18) follicular lymphoma (BCL-2); t(11;14) mantle cell (cyclin D1); t(11;22) Ewing sarcoma (EWS-FLI1); t(X;18) synovial sarcoma; t(12;21) childhood ALL (good outlook).
